(a) Recruit a sufficiently large, representative group of college students and randomly assign equal numbers to the new exercise program or to a control condition. Keep measurement procedures, study duration, and other treatment conditions the same, and compare the change in resting heart rate. Random assignment tends to balance confounders such as baseline fitness, age, sleep, medication use, diet, and other exercise between groups.

(b) Yes. Because measurement time may systematically affect heart rate, group students into morning and afternoon blocks and randomly assign treatment within each block. This controls time-of-day variation and improves precision.

(c) Test H₀: μprogram − μcontrol = 0 against Hₐ: μprogram − μcontrol < 0. The Welch statistic is t = (68 − 72)/√(6²/25 + 5²/25) = −2.56 with about 47 degrees of freedom. (d) The result is statistically significant, but practical significance requires subject-matter judgment: a 4-bpm reduction may or may not be large enough to be clinically meaningful, and its benefits should be weighed against cost and burden.

(a) The outcome probabilities are 1/20, 4/20, 5/20, and 10/20, so E(X) = 50(1/20) + 10(4/20) + 2(5/20) + 0(10/20) = $5.

(b) Because the $5 expected payout equals the $5 price to play, expected net gain is $0, so the game is fair in the long run. This is an average over many plays, not a guarantee for one play.

(c) E(X²) = 50²(1/20) + 10²(4/20) + 2²(5/20) + 0²(10/20) = 146, so Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 146 − 5² = 121 and SD(X) = √121 = $11.

(d) An $11 standard deviation is large relative to the $5 mean, consistent with outcomes ranging from $0 to $50. A game with the same mean and SD = $2 would have outcomes clustered much more tightly around $5 and would be less risky and more predictable.

(a) Interviewing people who happen to be at the mall is a nonrandom convenience sample, not an SRS of city residents.

(b) Location bias overrepresents mall visitors and underrepresents residents who shop online or do not visit the mall, likely making shopping-oriented views appear more common than citywide. (c) Draw an SRS from a comprehensive city-resident list using random numbers, or stratify by area and time window and randomly select residents within every stratum. Including residents beyond the mall reduces location bias, and sampling across evenings, weekdays, and weekends reduces schedule-based undercoverage.

(b) np = 12 and n(1−p) = 188 are both at least 10, so a Normal approximation is appropriate.

(c) Using continuity correction, P(X > 18) ≈ P(Y > 18.5) for Y ~ N(12, 3.359). The z-score is (18.5−12)/3.359 ≈ 1.935, so the probability is about 0.0265.

(d) Twenty-two defects are (22−12)/3.359 ≈ 2.98 standard deviations above the claimed mean, an unusually large count under p = 0.06. This rarity is evidence that the true defect rate may exceed 6%.
